Revision Techniques

Evidence-based strategies tailored to Enterprise and Marketing. The written exam rewards students who can recall named concepts precisely, apply them to a short start-up scenario, and build a justified chain of reasoning for the longer ‘analyse’ and ‘evaluate’ questions — these techniques are chosen to match exactly those demands.

Foundation Techniques

Start early — use these from day one
Active recall

Retrieval Practice

Test yourself on the seven entrepreneur characteristics, the four Ps, the five ownership types and the sales promotion techniques rather than re-reading. Brain dumps reveal exactly what you don’t know — and lock in what you do.

 Distributed practice

Spaced Repetition

Revisit cost classifications, break-even and the product lifecycle at 1, 3, 7, 14 and 30-day gaps. Works far better than cramming and stops the ‘I knew this last week’ feeling on exam day.

 Visual learning

Dual Coding

Combine words and visuals. A hand-drawn product lifecycle curve, a four-Ps spider diagram or a break-even graph sketched from memory sticks far better than text alone.

Stretch Techniques

Use these once you know the basics
Mixed practice

Interleaving

Mix entrepreneur, finance and marketing questions in one session. Trains you to identify which topic area a question targets — the exact skill the case-study Section B tests.

 Deep thinking

Elaborative Interrogation

Ask “why?” and “how?” about every fact. Why does market segmentation increase profit? How does a penetration price strategy affect cash flow? Turn memorised lists into understood explanations.

 Structured notes

Knowledge Organisers

One page per topic area. Named lists, definitions, formulas, worked examples. Redraw from memory. The base layer of solid exam preparation.

 Exam conditions

Timed Practice

Simulate the real thing. The written exam mixes quick recall with calculation questions and a 9-mark evaluation — practising under time pressure builds judgement about when to calculate and when to evaluate.

Evidence-based strategies tailored to GCSE Food Preparation and Nutrition (J587). PE rewards students who can recall precise terminology — cardiac output formulae, muscle fibre types, lever classifications — and apply that knowledge to unfamiliar practical scenarios. Paper 1 covers applied anatomy and physiology, health and fitness; Paper 2 covers sports psychology, socio-cultural influences, and health & fitness. Use the strategies below to build rock-solid recall across both papers.

Foundation Techniques

Start early — use these from day one
Active recall

Retrieval Practice

Test yourself on definitions, formulae, and classifications rather than re-reading. Brain dumps on “lever systems” or “components of fitness” reveal exactly what you don’t know — and strengthen what you do.

 Distributed practice

Spaced Repetition

Revisit the same material at 1, 3, 7, 14, 30-day gaps. Formulae like CO = SV × HR and the FITT principles need spacing to stick. Works better than cramming every time.

 Deep thinking

Elaborative Interrogation

Ask “why?” and “how?” to deepen understanding. Why does cardiac output increase during exercise? How does synovial fluid reduce friction? Turn memorised facts into understood physiology.

Consolidation Techniques

Use these once you know the basics
Visual learning

Dual Coding

Combine words and visuals. Annotated diagrams of the cardiovascular system, lever class flowcharts, and somatotype comparison tables stick far better than text alone — and PE is a highly visual subject.

 Mixed practice

Interleaving

Mix Paper 1 and Paper 2 topics in one session. Trains you to identify whether a question is testing anatomy, training principles, psychology, or socio-cultural factors — the discrimination skill the exam tests hardest.

 Structured notes

Knowledge Organisers

One page per topic. Key vocabulary, formulae, advantages/disadvantages, and worked examples. Redraw from memory. The base layer of every solid PE revision routine.

Exam Preparation

Final weeks — sharpen and apply
Exam conditions

Timed Practice

Simulate the real thing. OCR PE papers mix short-answer recall with extended 9-mark evaluations — practising under time pressure builds the judgement to switch between them confidently.

Evidence-based strategies tailored to Religious Studies A (8062). RE demands memorisation of quotes and teachings, two-sided argument writing, and precise religious vocabulary — these techniques are chosen to match exactly those demands.

Foundation Techniques

Active recall

Retrieval Practice

Test yourself on beliefs, teachings, and quotes rather than re-reading. Brain dumps on “Christian views on abortion” or “Islamic beliefs about Akhirah” reveal exactly what you don’t know — and strengthen what you do.

 Visual learning

Dual Coding

Combine words with visuals: comparison diagrams of Christian vs Muslim beliefs, annotated sketches of the Five Pillars, belief webs linking justice to sanctity of life. Visual encoding sticks far better than text alone.

 Deep questioning

Elaborative Interrogation

Ask “why” and “how” about everything. Why does the belief in Tawhid lead Muslims to oppose shirk? How does the Christian idea of the Trinity shape worship? Understanding the reasoning is what the 12-mark question rewards.

Religious Studies–Specific Techniques

Scripture memory

Quote Flashcards

RE rewards students who quote scripture accurately. Build a flashcard deck for Bible and Qur’an references — front: the quote or teaching, back: reference, religion, and how it supports a specific belief. Drill them with spaced repetition.

 Two religions

Comparison Tables

AQA asks you to compare Christian and Muslim beliefs on the same theme. Build a two-column table for every major topic — beliefs about God, life after death, marriage, justice — so similarities and differences are instantly retrievable.

 12-mark questions

Argument Planning

The 12-mark “Evaluate this statement” question is the hardest in the paper. Practise planning balanced arguments: two strong points for, two strong points against, each backed by a religious teaching, then a justified conclusion.

 Connecting ideas

Mind Mapping

RE topics are deeply interconnected — sanctity of life links to abortion, euthanasia, capital punishment, and just war. Mind mapping from a central belief outward reveals these connections and helps you write richer analytical answers.
